planting.note: Root detached leaves or pot offsets in a fast-draining succulent mix, grown in bright indirect light or light shade sheltered from hot midday sun.

directions: Gasteria barbae forms an elongate-triangular-leaved rosette marked with decorative white warty tubercles arranged in transverse zebra-like bands, and the foliage takes on a reddish flush during dry, sunnier spells. It is endemic to a narrow stretch of South Africa's Western Cape between Knysna and Robberg, where it grows tucked among coastal scrub. The leaves are notably brittle; a detached leaf will callus over quickly and root to form a new plantlet, making leaf propagation an easy option alongside division of offsets. Grow in a gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in bright indirect light or light shade, since plants raised in shade produce longer, greener leaves while full-sun specimens stay shorter and more compact, and water only once the soil has dried out completely.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Pot offsets or rooted leaf cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix; grow in a shallow pan or crevice planting to mimic its cliff-ledge habitat, in bright indirect light or light shade.

directions: Described only in 2020, Gasteria camillae is an obligate cliff-dweller confined to the eastern Baviaanskloof mountains of South Africa's Eastern Cape, where it roots directly into rock crevices and ledges. It is closely related to Gasteria glauca but is distinguished by a short, upright stem, smaller rosettes, and smooth, non-warty leaf surfaces at every growth stage rather than the tuberculate texture typical of many gasterias. The greyish-green, keeled leaves are densely packed rather than arranged in the flat two-ranked fans seen in some relatives, an adaptation that helps the plant endure long, semi-arid dry spells on exposed rock faces. In cultivation, mimic its native ledge habitat with a shallow, extremely fast-draining gritty mix, bright indirect light or light shade, and water sparingly, letting the mix dry fully between waterings.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Divide basal offsets or root detached leaves in fast-draining succulent mix; grow in bright indirect light or light shade and expect autumn rather than summer bloom.

directions: Gasteria koenii is a stemless species restricted to the southern foothills of the Groot Swartberg near Calitzdorp in South Africa, where it forms prolific clustering clumps of three to eight rosette heads. Its long, narrow, sickle-shaped leaves are mottled and leathery, smooth-surfaced and drawn out to a tapering point, distinguishing it from the shorter, broader, often tuberculate leaves of neighboring gasteria species. Like other members of the genus, its brittle leaves root readily when detached, forming new plantlets and offering an easy backup propagation method to division. Notably, it is one of the few gasterias that flowers in autumn rather than summer, sending up an unbranched raceme of small, pendent, orange-red to pinkish blooms. Grow in a gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in bright indirect light or light shade, watering only once the mix has dried completely.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Pot offsets in lean, fast-draining succulent mix and grow in bright indirect light or light shade beneath the dappled cover of a nearby shrub, as it does in the wild.

directions: Gasteria langebergensis was raised from a variety of Gasteria disticha to full species status in 2019 and is endemic to shale slopes of the Bokkeveld Group between Worcester and Robertson in South Africa's Western Cape. It is a compact, ground-hugging succulent readily told apart from typical G. disticha by its smaller, narrower leaves with distinctly toothed margins and a matt rather than glossy leaf surface. In habitat it grows in the dappled shade cast by low nurse shrubs of the Succulent Karoo, an arrangement worth mimicking in cultivation with bright indirect light or light shade rather than harsh, unfiltered sun. Plant in a lean, sharply drained gritty mix and water only once the soil has dried out fully, since prolonged dampness is far more likely to kill it than drought.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Pot small offsets in a shallow pan of fast-draining gritty mix to suit its dwarf, cliff-ledge habit; grow in bright indirect light or light shade.

directions: One of the smallest species in the genus, Gasteria doreeniae is a dwarf, virtually stemless cliff-dweller endemic to the Swartwaterspoort of South Africa's Eastern Cape, where it clings to narrow rock ledges and scree at 350 to 500 meters elevation. It forms dense, ascending clusters rarely more than about six inches across, made up of short, belt-shaped leaves arranged in two opposite ranks that stand upright when young and spread outward with incurved tips as the dry season progresses. Its diminutive scale and slow, clumping growth make it well suited to shallow pans or crevice-style succulent plantings rather than deep pots. Grow in an especially fast-draining gritty mix in bright indirect light or light shade, and water sparingly, letting the mix dry out completely between waterings to guard against rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Pot offsets or rooted leaf cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix and grow in bright indirect light or light shade, protecting from intense direct midday sun.

directions: Gasteria nitida, whose species name means 'shiny' for its glossy leaf surface, is a variable, stemless succulent native to a stretch of South Africa's Eastern and Western Cape between Uniondale and the Great Fish River mouth. Smooth, triangular leaves are arranged in loose spiral or two-ranked rosettes and are dark green with irregular transverse bands of white spotting, though juvenile leaves often show a rougher, tuberculate texture that smooths out with age. It grows solitary or slowly proliferates from the base into a small clump, and produces bright reddish-pink, yellow-throated flowers on simple or branched racemes in summer. Grow in a fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light or light shade, and water only once the soil has dried out completely, reducing watering further through the winter months.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Divide rooted rhizome offsets and pot in fast-draining cactus or succulent mix; grow in bright indirect light to partial sun and keep on the dry side, especially over winter.

directions: Dracaena hallii, long known as Sansevieria hallii and commonly nicknamed the baseball bat plant, is native to dry savanna and bushveld in southeastern Zimbabwe and Mozambique's border region with Limpopo Province, South Africa, where it is confined mostly to rocky, sandstone-derived soils in dry river valleys. It produces extraordinarily thick, rounded, club-like leaves with a shallow central channel that curve gently rather than standing rigidly upright, giving each rosette a bulky, sculptural profile quite unlike the flat, sword-shaped leaves of common snake plant. Dense heads of flowers are carried on short stems close to the foliage rather than on tall separate spikes. Grow in a very fast-draining gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light to partial sun, and let the soil dry out completely between waterings, since its thick water-storing leaves are especially prone to rot in damp conditions.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Bally's Dwarf Snake Plant (Stoloniferous Dwarf Sansevieria)

planting.note: Separate rooted stolon offsets and pot in fast-draining succulent mix; grow in bright indirect light to partial sun as a small container or dish-garden plant.

directions: Dracaena ballyi, formerly and still often sold as Sansevieria ballyi, is a diminutive East African species native to southern Kenya and Tanzania that spreads by wiry stolons connecting small, symmetrical rosettes rather than growing as a single clumping crown. Each rosette holds a handful of stiff, nearly cylindrical, recurved leaves in dark green with light green cross-banding and a sharp reddish-brown tip, reaching only a few inches long. Because new rosettes form and root along the spreading stolons, a single plant gradually colonizes the surface of a shallow pot, making it well suited to dish gardens and mixed succulent bowls. It tolerates a wide range of light from full sun to fairly low light, though bright filtered light produces the best color and habit; water about once a week during active growth, letting the top inch of mix dry between waterings, and less in winter.
